title: Enmei Jukku Kannon Gyo
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: The talk emphasizes the importance of cultivating self-compassion, particularly in Buddhism, by recognizing our own inherent suffering and imperfection. Through the story of Heigaku Talus Latona's personal experience with Kanzeon, the Bodhisattva of Compassion, we see that embracing our vulnerabilities is a key aspect of developing compassion for ourselves. This understanding is rooted in the 10 Verses for Protecting Life Bodhisattva Sutra, which encourages us to recognize the interconnectedness of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha as our transcending cause, leading to freedom from suffering through acceptance and purity.
topics: 10 Verses for Protecting Life Bodhisattva Sutra

sentences.text: Hi.

December 23rd was the 20th anniversary of my father's death, and two weeks before that, we were getting set up for Rohatsu, for our Buddhist Enlightenment celebration, where I was head cook for the first time.

That Thursday afternoon I got a call from my mother saying, "Hey, could you fly out to Colorado on the 23rd so that we can, with her and my brother and I, climb the mountain where we scattered his ashes?"

I was pretty deep into figuring out preparations for Rohatsu, and this was also the time that we had that big cold snap, so there was a lot of extra work that needed doing that I was not carrying my share of at home.
But family's important, and they're there when I need them, and I said sure.

About a week before the 23rd, I got a cold, but it pretty much passed, so I went ahead and flew to Colorado, climbed that mountain, and then spent the next two days carrying my niece and nephew up and down the stairs for fun.
My body didn't quite like that after that cold.
It came back with a vengeance, and I was out of work for a few days, again with more work piling up at home.
So I got a good amount of rest, but I really needed to get some chores done, so I went down to the pasture to pick up manure.
Now I also get migraine headaches on occasion, and they often come with a visual aura, sparkly lights.
This particular time the aura decided to be right in the center of my vision.
Sometimes it's off to the side, but this was...

So I couldn't breathe because my nose was stuffed, and I was coughing all over the place, and my right ear infection was pounding, and I couldn't see what I was doing, so I was just slapping manure all over.
I couldn't see the bucket.
And among all that, a very Zen thought arose.
And this is the thought that arose: "Poor me."
Do you ever feel that way?
Poor me.
Everybody say it with me.
One, two, three.
Poor me.
Now that was pathetic, but it wasn't pathetic enough.
Let's try one more time.
Really pathetic now.
Poor me.
Poor me is okay.
That's honest, at least.
Our challenge is not to get caught up in it, not to get stuck in poor me.
A lot of times we talk about how compassion is central to Buddhism, and we usually throw in the observation, "Don't forget compassion for yourself."
But let's be brutally honest, let's face it: the first reason that most of us are here is to ease our own distress.
We don't generally come to Buddhism saying, "I want to be compassionate to all living beings."
It usually starts at home.
And that's where Kanzeon comes in.
We've been doing this series of talks about the chants in the chant book, and tonight we're talking about the Enmeijuku Kanan-gyo, the third chant that we chanted tonight.
Kanan there is Kanzeon, also known as Guan Yin, also known as Avalokiteshvara.
That's the one who hears the cries of the world, and there are half a dozen other versions of that name and translations.
Elihu Genmyo Smith, the first Dharma heir of Charlotte Joko Beck, says it's the one perceiving and responding to suffering.
So this Kanzeon perceives the suffering of all beings and responds to it.
And one of the important aspects that's consistent throughout all these names and all these translations is that this compassion for us is without judgment.
It's not just a reward for being good, it's compassion, acceptance of us, who we are.
There's Kanzeon.
If you look close, oftentimes the statues are shown with 11 heads.
And the legend, the tradition there, is that with all of the cries in the world, and there is a bit of suffering in the world, with all of those cries of suffering, one head just wasn't enough.
So one of the Buddhas gave her another 10 heads to try and handle it all.
And then one set of arms isn't enough, one set of hands for healing, so she's often shown with more arms, more hands.
I'm using "she" as the current gender utilization; in pre-1000 BC it was typically "he."
I think it's probably appropriate to observe that compassion is genderless.
It would be difficult to tiptoe through this discussion of Kanzeon without examining one of our favorite koans about her 11 heads and four or six or however many arms.
This is case number 105 in Dogen's Shobogenzo.
It's important enough that it also appears in the Blue Cliff Record and the Book of Serenity.
We've talked about it before.
*Yunyan asked Daowu, "How does the Bodhisattva of great compassion use so many hands and eyes?"
Daowu said, "It's just like a person in the middle of the night reaching back in search of a pillow."
"How hard is that?"
Yunyan said, "I understand."
Daowu asked, "How do you understand it?"
And Yunyan said, "All over the body are hands and eyes."*
*Daowu said, "What you said is all right, but that's only 80% of it."
Yunyan said, "I am like this.
Senior brother, how do you understand it?"
Daowu said, "Throughout the body are hands and eyes."*
Our guiding teacher Norman Fischer goes so far as to say, the body is nothing but hands and eyes, perceiving and responding to suffering.
Well, the chant that we're chanting is about 1500 years old. 400 years ago our Zen ancestor Hakuin was a staunch advocate of people chanting this chant.
The Japanese comes from the Chinese, and the Chinese form is not a translation but a transliteration of the sounds chanted in Sanskrit, the ancient language of Buddhism.
And the chant is a response to the Lotus Sutra, which is about 2000 years old.
I'll grab you a bit from chapter 25.
Here she's called the Regarder of the Cries of the World.
Shakyamuni Buddha says:

*If there were countless hundreds of thousands of billions of living beings, experiencing suffering and agony, who heard this Regarder of the Cries of the World Bodhisattva, and wholeheartedly called her name, Regarder of the Cries of the World Bodhisattva would immediately hear those cries, and all of them would be freed.

If anyone who embraces the name of Regarder of the Cries of the World Bodhisattva falls into a great fire, the fire will not burn that person due to the divine authority and power of that Bodhisattva.
If anyone carried away by a flood calls her name, that person will immediately reach some shallows.

Or if someone faced with immediate attack calls the name of Regarder of the Cries of the World Bodhisattva, the swords and clubs of the attackers will instantly break into pieces, and they will be freed from the danger.*

*Even if the great three thousand, great thousand-fold world were full of satyrs and ogres seeking to torment people, these evil spirits, hearing the people call the name, Regarder of the Cries of the World Bodhisattva, with their wicked eyes they would not even be able to see them, these satyrs and ogres, much less hurt them.

If moreover someone guilty or not guilty is captured and put in stocks or manacles and chains, and they call the name Regarder of the Cries of the World Bodhisattva, their bonds will be broken, and they will be freed.*
*If any living beings are afflicted with a great deal of lust, let them keep in mind and revere Regarder of the Cries of the World Bodhisattva, and they will be freed from their desire.
If they have a great deal of anger and rage, let them keep in mind and revere Regarder of the Cries of the World Bodhisattva, and they will be freed from their anger.
If they are deluded by great folly, let them keep in mind and revere Regarder of the Cries of the World Bodhisattva, and they will be freed from their stupidity.*
Out of that arose the tradition, the practice, of calling on Guanyin, on Kanzeon, for help.
You might take a literal or a philosophical, more metaphorical understanding of this.
The Zen approach is understanding that there is no self to be found which is separate from pure compassion in every world.
So our demons evaporate as our vision clears.

Now whether you take the metaphysical understanding, the metaphorical understanding, or the literal understanding of calling on compassionate acceptance, our Dharma practice calls on us to soften our certainty about which is true, that in enlightened practice there's both, both the philosophical understanding and [unclear: "personal availence"].
A lot of our Japanese chants are not translated, but if you look at page 9, this one is.
This translation is by Robert Aitken, and he discusses some of the choices he made in translating in the book The Morning Star.
Starting out with the title, the Enmei Jukku Kanangyo could be translated as the Ten Verses for Protecting Life Bodhisattva of Compassion Sutra.
We often say protecting life; Aiken points out that timeless life might be another translation.
The essential timeless nature which is not born and does not die includes the morning star and the peach blossoms.
So we have the first line:
*Kanzeon!*
With an exclamation point, calling out.
Kanzeon, come.
*Regarder of the cries of the world, Bodhisattva of Compassion, come.*
The next line says:
*I venerate the Buddha.*
Which Buddha is that?
Well, we just called the name of Buddha.
And of course, any reference to Buddha is a reference to the possibility of clear living without suffering.
*Buddha is my source.
Buddha is my affinity.*
Now the words that are translated here as source and affinity are opposites.
We might not in English think of them as opposites, but the words they came from were opposites, and therefore they are all-inclusive.
Buddha is everything: the direct cause and the transcending cause.
The next line is:
*Affinity with Buddha, Dharma and Sangha.*
The three treasures, of course.
So the source and affinity are our transcending cause.
Buddha, the harmonious life, the possibility of clarity; Dharma, the practice and the teaching and how we go about our practice; and the Sangha, this community that we are, is our transcending cause.
The next line says:
*Constancy, ease, assurance and purity.*
These are known as the four freedoms.
Constancy is the freedom from time, ease the freedom from distress, assurance the freedom from bondage, and purity the freedom from delusion.
They're the four attributes of nirvana.
*Morning, my thought is Kanzeon.*
That word "thought": Nomon Tim Burnett proposed the translation "deep yearning for connection."
Morning, my deep yearning for connection is Kanzeon.
Enlightenment goes beyond this thought, beyond this yearning, but we are not beyond this thought, beyond this yearning.
And Avalokiteshvara offers it to us without judgment.
Note the wording of that line: my thought is Kanzeon, not "I'm thinking about Kanzeon in the morning," but in the morning my thought is compassion.
*Evening, my thought is Kanzeon.*
Morning thought, evening thought.
Since the recorder battery just died, we'll finish up the talk without the studio audience.
Morning, my thought is Kanzeon.
Evening, my thought is Kanzeon.
This brings to mind case three of the Blue Cliff Record.
*Great Master Ba was unwell.
The chief monk of the temple came to ask him, "Master, how do you feel these days?"
Great Master Ba said, "Sun-faced Buddha, moon-faced Buddha."*
What did the master mean?
When it's bright out, my thought is Kanzeon.
When it's dark out, my thought is Kanzeon.
When I'm sick, my thought is Kanzeon.
When I'm vigorous, my thought is Kanzeon.
Living only 24 hours like moon-faced Buddha, my thought is Kanzeon.
Living 1,800 years like sun-faced Buddha, my thought is Kanzeon.
Then this brings us back to our earlier use of protecting life and timeless life as synonyms.
The next line:
*Thought after thought arises in mind.*
Huh.
*Thought after thought arises in mind.*
*Thought after thought arises in mind.*
Has anyone here ever experienced that?
Yeah, when we sit and this happens, it's not something wrong.
The sutra is just observing: this is what happens.
Thought after thought arises in mind.
And the next line:
*Thought after thought is not separate from mind.*
That's what mind is.
That's what minds do, is think.
But that's not what we are.
Not this limited mind.
Sometimes all we can manage, desperately trying to keep Dharma in mind, is just *Kanzeon namubutsu yobutsu u en yobutsu u* and on.
And to keep on with that, being miserable, being pathetic, I'll finish with some words from Merle Kodo Boyd, who is the guiding teacher of the Lincroft Zen Sangha in the White Plum Lineage.
She says:
*The only thing that can make us uncomfortable with being alone is not liking who we are.
That's what we do when we face the wall.
We face who we are.
Being okay with however that arises is the most compassion and the most honesty you can ever offer yourself.*
Just to accept yourself as you are.
Even if you don't like it, that's okay.
Because not okay is always a practice gate.
We can always include what we don't like in ourselves.
But letting go of worrying about having to become perfect, that's a gift we can give to ourselves.
Thank you.
